Abstract
The convergence of edge computing, big data analytics, and ar-
tificial intelligence (AI) with traditional scientific calculations is
increasingly being adopted in high-performance computing (HPC)
workflows. Workflow management systems are crucial for manag-
ing and orchestrating these complex computational tasks. However,
it is difficult to identify patterns within the growing population
of HPC workflows. Moreover, serverless has emerged as a novel
computing paradigm, offering dynamic resource allocation, quick
response time, fine-grained resource management and auto-scaling.
In this tutorial, we present a framework to evaluate serverless execu-
tions of HPC scientific workflows. Our approach integrates a widely
used traditional HPC workflow generator with an HPC serverless
workflow management system to create benchmark suites of scien-
tific workflows with diverse characteristics.

Introduction
As scientific applications become more modern, they combine
different scientific domains, such as machine learning applications
that combine a range of domains like data science and statistics, for
training and learning algorithms. Scientific workflows have become
more popular in that sense, being critical in managing and orches-
trating complex computational tasks across diverse domains [5].
These workflows, consisting of interdependent tasks, enable sci-
entists to process large volumes of data, automate analyses, and
derive meaningful insights with high efficiency [10].
Recent efforts have leveraged serverless computing for scientific
workflows, particularly in HPC [4, 16]. Serverless computing can fa-
cilitate the application development process, simplify management,
and reduce costs while providing on-demand resource provisioning
and automatic scalability. Examples of such applications include
genomics data processing, large-scale simulation workflows, and
real-time data analysis in environmental sciences [13], where server-
less paradigms can significantly streamline execution and resource
allocation while maintaining the computational rigor required by
HPC workloads.
The combination of HPC and serverless computing has driven
a wide range of efforts and objectives, including the design of re-
source management and scheduling algorithms, the development
of runtime systems capable of executing workflows across various
hardware and software stacks, and the analysis of workflow configu-
rations to identify commonalities and differences between scientific
domains [6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15]. However, the existing literature on
HPC serverless workflows lacks a comprehensive framework that
bridges the theoretical and practical aspects of workflow managers’
research and development. Most experimental evaluations of these
workflows rely on real-world workflow instances.
Figure 1: Architecture of WfCommons.
WfCommons [7] has been a pivotal framework for the scien-
tific workflow community, enabling scientists to study and explore
hypothetical and future scenarios on testbed platforms, without
requiring real-world and production workflows1. WfCommons of-
fers tools and data to cater to research and development needs by
making real-world workflow instances accessible through a com-
mon format and generating realistic workflow benchmark speci-
fications. In this tutorial, we will focus on the realistic workflow
benchmarking component called WfBench. WfBench generates
realistic workflow benchmark specifications that can be translated
into benchmark code to be executed with various current workflow
systems. It enables the generation of workflow tasks with arbitrary

performance characteristics (CPU, memory, and I/O usage) and
realistic task dependency structures, based on observed produc-
tion workflows. The generation of benchmarks is twofold. First,
a realistic workflow benchmark specification is created, and then
this specification is translated into benchmark code to be executed
with a workflow system. We have recently equipped WfCommons
with the tools to advance the research and development of server-
less workflows (see Figure 1), especially those tailored for HPC
environments [4].
In this tutorial, we will also detail this integration and go through
how it works step by step. Our approach includes adapting the
WfCommons framework to generate serverless-compatible HPC
workflow benchmarks and developing a new workflow manager
specifically designed for HPC serverless environments, named Hy-
brid Serverless Management Flow framework (HSMFlow). This
comprehensive framework enables more extensive research into
the performance and applicability of serverless computing within
the scientific workflow domain.
The HSMFlow framework [1], available on GitHub, and illus-
trated in Figure 2, is composed of four main components. By com-
bining our workflow manager (component 3), which is capable of
executing workflows on any serverless platform that handles HTTP
requests from any cluster (component 4), with our contribution
to WfCommons (component 1), we can perform an extensive set
of experiments with scientific workflows on serverless platforms
(component 2). In these experiments, we vary the size of the work-
flows, the amount of CPU each function should stress, the choice of
whether to keep or release memory allocated during the execution
of the functions, and the granularity of the serverless processes.
Figure 2: Architecture of HSMFlow.
In this tutorial, we will show how to generate several different
scientific workflows, varying their CPU, memory, and network
charges and requirements, as well as their sizes [3]. Then, we will
show how to translate the generated workflows into the desired
platform format, which is Knative in our case [2]. We will briefly
present our chosen serverless platform, Knative, and demonstrate
how to operate it minimally. We will also show how we deploy
WfBench as a service in the Knative serverless platform. Following
the execution flow, we will show how to individually invoke such
a service (WfBench), and then how to use the HSMFlow to execute
entire workflows. Finally, we will show how to extract measure-
ments from the serverless platform and plot performance metrics.
All demonstrations will be conducted on the National Data Platform
(NDP) 2, a community-driven, open platform that provides shared
2National Data Platform: https://nationaldataplatform.org/
infrastructure and services to support data-intensive science across
various domains. The NDP enables researchers to access scalable
computing resources, standardized data services, and interoperable
tools in a federated environment, making it an ideal foundation for
experimenting with serverless workflow execution at scale. During
the tutorial, participants will log in to the NDP using their individ-
ual accounts, where they will access workspaces that will host all
the necessary materials, datasets, and computing resources. This
setup ensures that attendees can follow the hands-on exercises
seamlessly and reproduce the demonstrated workflows within their
own isolated environments.
Therefore, our main contributions are the demonstrations of:
• How to manage scientific workflows in Serverless Comput-
ing, using the HSMFlow framework;
• How to generate HPC scientific workflows for serverless
using the WfCommons framework;
• How to integrate both frameworks, HSMFlow and WfCom-
mons;
• A tutorial, conducted using a real-world deployed server-
less platform, with a collection of examples of generated
HPC scientific workflows, executed in a WFM framework
for serverless computing.
2
Tutorial Outline
In this tutorial, we will:
(1) Introduce scientific workflows and the WfCommons Frame-
work;
(2) Introduce Serverless Computing and the Knative open-source
serverless platform;
(3) Demonstrate how to generate synthetic workflow bench-
marks with WfCommons;
(4) Introduce the WfCommons Knative Translator component,
and demonstrate how to translate a generic-formatted work-
flow to the Knative Platform;
(5) Introduce the HSMFlow framework for managing workflows
in serverless;
(6) Demonstrate how to execute the generated workflows on
Knative, using the HSMFlow framework in the National Data
Platform;
(7) Demonstrate how to monitor serverless execution on Kna-
tive;
(8) Demonstrate how to retrieve experiment results;
(9) Demonstrate how to analyze and plot the generated data.
